title: A small neural network that spots leukemia cells with a fifth of the parameters
paper_title: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Classification using Compact Channel Specific Multi-column CNNs
date_note: CODEC 2023 (8th Int. Conf. on Computers and Devices for Communication), Kolkata, 14-16 Dec 2023
venue: 8th International Conference on Computers and Devices for Communication (CODEC)
authors: R Satpathi, S Das, M Laha, Swarnendu Ghosh
summary: A small multi-column network tells leukemia cells from healthy ones in microscope images, matching a much larger ensemble to within 1.3 accuracy points while using about a fifth of its parameters.

body.p: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is a cancer of the blood and bone marrow. Early screening matters, and we wanted a neural network that could tell leukemic cells from healthy ones in microscope images without needing a huge model. Our network does this with 7.5 million parameters, about a fifth of the size of the best published model we compared against.

In this disease the bone marrow makes too many immature white blood cells, called lymphoblasts, which crowd out healthy blood cells. It is the most common leukemia in children, about 25% of pediatric cancer diagnoses by the paper's figure. We used the ISBI 2019 C-NMC challenge dataset, which has segmented images of lymphoblasts: 10,661 training images from 73 patients and 1,867 test images from 28 patients.

Two things shape the task. Staining the cells introduces colour differences that have nothing to do with the cell itself, and we wanted the network to focus on the cell rather than the pigment. The second is size. Some published results reach high accuracy with a huge number of parameters and extra overhead, and the paper argues that a network has to be compact before it can be deployed in real life. A parameter is one learned number inside the network, so a count of parameters is a rough measure of size.

We split each colour image into its three channels, red, green and blue, and gave each its own small network, or column. Looking at one channel at a time pushes the network to attend to variations in intensity rather than the colour tint. The model has two phases. The first has three layers of channel-specific feature extraction. Then the three outputs are joined, and the second phase has three more layers that work on the combined features. For training we used standard data augmentation: linear transformations, added noise, and random changes in intensity and colour.

To keep the model small, we built it from depth-wise separable convolutions. In each block a 1 × 1 step first maps the features to more channels, and then one or more 3 × 3 steps handle the spatial pattern. Max pooling shrinks the image between blocks. In the last block a 7 × 7 average pooling turns the spatial features into a flat vector for a small classifier, a multi-layer perceptron.

figure.caption: The three colour channels get their own early layers (left). The features are then concatenated and processed together before the classifier (right).

body.p: The network reached 97.5% test accuracy, with precision 0.973 and recall 0.972. The state-of-the-art model we compared against combines DenseNet121, ResNet50 and MobileNet with a random forest, a second classifier that works on their outputs. It scored 98.8% with 38 million parameters, plus the overhead of that second classifier. Even against this top model our network loses only 1.3% in accuracy, with almost five times fewer parameters, and it needs no additional classifier.

body.callout: 97.5% accuracy with 7.5 million parameters, against 98.8% with 38 million for the state-of-the-art model.

body.p: The standard networks on their own scored lower. DenseNet121 (8.1 million parameters) reached 94.00%, ResNet50 (25.6 million) 93.50% and MobileNet (4.3 million) 94.20% (Table 1). The paper concludes that, in its experiments, models of comparable size perform much worse than ours.
All results come from one dataset, the ISBI 2019 C-NMC challenge data. We did not test other datasets, and the paper reports no experiments on images from other sources.
Our conclusion is that the model meets two aims together: it counters staining artefacts and stays small. That makes it more suitable for real-world deployment than the large ensembles.
